summary.text: Proteins are large molecules made of one or more long chains of amino acid residues.
They do many jobs in living things, including speeding up reactions, copying DNA, giving cells structure and moving molecules around.
A protein's amino acid sequence, set by its gene, usually makes it fold into a specific 3D structure that determines its activity.

facts.label: Short chains
facts.value: Under 20–30 residues, usually called peptides instead

facts.label: Standard amino acids
facts.value: The genetic code specifies 20 of them

facts.label: Muscle proteins
facts.value: Actin and myosin give muscle its mechanical function

items.prompt: A lab isolates a chain of only 12 amino acid residues. What is such a short chain commonly called?

options.label: A cofactor
A peptide
A proteasome
A protein complex

items.explain: Chains of fewer than 20–30 residues are rarely considered proteins and are commonly called peptides.

items.prompt: Two proteins in the same cell do very different jobs. What mostly sets them apart?

options.label: How many cofactors each one carries
The time of day each one is made
The size of the cell they sit in
The order of their amino acids

items.explain: Proteins differ mainly in their amino acid sequence, which comes from the sequence of their genes.

items.prompt: A cell finds a protein that is misfolded and damaged. Compared with a healthy one, how is it handled?

options.label: It is broken down faster than usual
It is kept longer as a spare
It is rebuilt into a new gene
It is left alone until it wears out

items.explain: Abnormal or misfolded proteins are degraded more rapidly, often by the proteasome.

items.prompt: An enzyme only works when a non-protein ion or compound helps it. What are such helpers called?

options.label: Half-lives
Peptides
Cofactors
Albumins

items.explain: Proteins that need a non-protein compound or ion for activity depend on what are known as cofactors.

items.prompt: Biochemists talk about a protein's half-life. What does it measure?

options.label: How quickly it folds into its final shape
How long it lasts before the cell breaks it down
How many amino acid residues it holds
How much energy it gives off as it works

items.explain: Proteins exist for a certain period and are then degraded and recycled; their lifespan is measured as a half-life.

items.prompt: Why must animals eat protein as part of their diet?

options.label: To get essential amino acids the body cannot make
To get the cofactors every enzyme needs to start
To replace the water that cells lose each day
To supply the genes that cells read to build molecules

items.explain: Animals need dietary protein to provide essential amino acids that they cannot make themselves.
